results.title: AI-bioinformatics synergy for precision medicine in brain diseases: integrating radiomics and multi-omics data
results.summary:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
<jats:p>The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and bioinformatics is reshaping the landscape of precision medicine in brain diseases, particularly in neurological diseases and brain tumors. Despite advances in both fields, the combined application of radiomics and multi-omics fusion remains underutilized, even though integrative frameworks are essential for addressing the complexity and heterogeneity of imaging and molecular data. This review examines how integrative AI-bioinformatics frameworks enable the fusion of radiomics with genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and other omics modalities to more comprehensively model disease complexity. Leveraging deep learning, graph neural networks, and advanced representation learning, these multimodal systems facilitate biomarker discovery, patient stratification, and personalized treatment strategies. We critically evaluate key challenges including data heterogeneity, limited interpretability, and barriers to clinical validation, and highlight emerging solutions aimed at enhancing reproducibility and translational readiness. Case studies in gliomas, Alzheimer’s disease, and multiple sclerosis illustrate the clinical utility of unified imaging-omics architectures. Ultimately, this review positions radiomics and multi-omics integration as a foundational approach for the next generation of precision medicine in brain diseases by bridging the gap between computational innovation and clinical application.</jats:p>

results.title: Management of Urinary Symptoms in Multiple Sclerosis: An Umbrella Review
results.summary:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Background</jats:title>
<jats:p>Lower urinary tract dysfunctions (LUTDs) are prevalent among patients with multiple sclerosis (MS), which is the most common immune‐mediated neurologic disease among the juvenile population. This study aims to evaluate the efficacy and safety of different methods in the management of MS‐related LUTD.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
<jats:p>This study was conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses (PRISMA) statement and Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methods. Systematic review studies that reported the efficacy of any management method for LUTD in MS are considered for inclusion. A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Embase, and Web of Science and risk of bias was assessed using the JBI critical appraisal checklist for systematic reviews.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Results</jats:title>
<jats:p>Out of 342 screened records, 34 systematic reviews were included. Preliminary efficacy and safety of pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) and tibial nerve stimulation (TNS), as well as the potential of alpha‐blockers, cannabinoids, mirabegron, spinal cord stimulation, sacral neuromodulation, transcranial neuromodulations, vaginal/rectal and clitoral/penile stimulation, foot reflexology, craniosacral therapy, and stem cell therapy were suggested. Despite the appropriate efficacy, anticholinergics, desmopressin, intradetrusor injections of botulinum toxin A, vanilloids, and catheterization were found to cause considerable side effects.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
<jats:p>Despite a high prevalence of LUTDs in MS patients, evidence basis of the management methods is still poor and there is lack of well‐designed randomized controlled trials, which makes evidence inconclusive. Future research is needed to refine treatment algorithms, investigate the potential of combination therapies, and develop individualized treatment paradigms.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>

results.title: Validation of generative artificial intelligence techniques for synthetic data generation in multiple sclerosis research: A comparison with real-world evidence from the Italian multiple sclerosis registry
results.summary:
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Background:</jats:title>
<jats:p>The use of generative artificial intelligence to create synthetic data is an emerging strategy to enhance real-world evidence.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Objective:</jats:title>
<jats:p>To assess the validity of artificial intelligence-generated synthetic data in replicating data collected in the Italian Multiple Sclerosis and Related Disorders Register for the evaluation of progression independent of relapse activity risk under early intensive treatment and escalation treatment strategies.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Methods:</jats:title>
<jats:p>Artificial intelligence generative models were trained on a sub-cohort of 1666 Italian Multiple Sclerosis and Related Disorders Register patients to generate a synthetic dataset of 4878 patients. Synthetic vAlidation FramEwork, Clinical Synthetic Fidelity, and Nearest Neighbor Distance Ratio were applied. Comparisons between treatment strategies were conducted using both real and synthetic data, focusing on progression independent of relapse activity risk.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
<jats:p>The synthetic data demonstrated fidelity and privacy preservation. Treatment-effect estimates for escalation treatment versus early intensive treatment were similar across the real and synthetic datasets. Cox proportional hazards models showed that synthetic data preserved the robustness of the estimates for the risk of a first progression independent of relapse activity event. Associations with radiological risk factors were broadly similar across the real and synthetic datasets.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Conclusion:</jats:title>
<jats:p>Artificial intelligence-generated synthetic data reliably replicated treatment-effect outcomes of Italian Multiple Sclerosis and Related Disorders Register data, supporting their potential use in clinically defined research settings.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>

results.title: Multi-scale Gaussian product-of-experts for missing sequence multiple sclerosis lesion segmentation
results.summary:
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
<jats:p>To develop and evaluate a unified framework for multiple sclerosis (MS) white matter lesion segmentation that operates robustly under clinically prevalent missing sequence magnetic resonance imaging conditions.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
<jats:p>We propose a multi-scale Gaussian product-of-experts framework (MG-PoE) integrated into nnU-Net, where sequence-specific inputs are independently processed through a shared encoder and parameterized as Gaussian experts before combination through precision-weighted product-of-experts (PoE) fusion at each encoder scale. The unified fusion rule handles different sequence configurations without requiring subset-specific architectures. The framework was systematically evaluated under different sequence configurations on diverse datasets (MSSEG2016, MS3SEG, and MSLesSeg24).</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Results</jats:title>
<jats:p>On the five-sequence MSSEG2016, the proposed framework achieved the best overall performance compared to benchmark methods across all full-sequence and partially observed multisequence settings, with a mean Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 0.7029, a mean 95th percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) of 22.4030, and a mean Composite Score (CS) of 0.7235 across the 26 sequence configurations. On MS3SEG, MG-PoE achieved the highest mean DSC and CS across the full sequence and missing-sequence settings, with significant improvements over competing methods, while HD95 performance was generally comparable. In zero-shot evaluation on MSLesSeg24, the method achieved the best overall DSC and HD95 in the full sequence setting (DSC, 0.5566; HD95, 27.3729) and the best mean DSC, HD95 and CS across the missing-sequence settings (DSC, 0.5096; HD95, 30.5054; CS, 0.5811).</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
<jats:p>The MG-PoE framework provides a unified approach to missing-sequence MS lesion segmentation, achieving favorable performance on independent datasets and providing initial evidence of cross-dataset robustness.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>

Published research and clinical trials for myelin.

This category includes research on myelin structure, myelin sheath repair, remyelination processes, demyelination mechanisms, and myelin regeneration therapies. Key research areas include oligodendrocytes, oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCs), Schwann cells, white matter pathology, CNS and PNS myelin, myelin proteins (MBP, PLP, MOG), and therapeutic approaches for myelin repair and remyelination.
